content: 1. The date of the first prescribed antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be recorded, along with the date and value of the first viral load test. Follow-up viral load test dates and values should also be documented. 2. The date of death and the primary cause of death should be included in the records. Deaths among individuals with HIV infection should be reported, regardless of whether they meet the clinical criteria for AIDS. 3. Viral suppression is defined as a viral load of less than 1,000 copies per milliliter. 4. In settings where viral load tests are conducted routinely, they are typically performed six months after ART initiation and annually thereafter. The date of ART initiation is considered six months prior to the first viral load test. 5. Currently on ART refers to individuals who initiated ART and remained on treatment during the reporting period. 6. ART retention can be estimated by the number of individuals receiving follow-up viral load measurements. 7. HIV case surveillance uses standardized criteria to determine whether an HIV case should be reported. This ensures comparability of data across different settings. 8. WHO updated its clinical staging and surveillance case definitions for HIV in 2007, covering both adults and children. Prior to this, only AIDS cases were reported, which did not provide a complete picture of the epidemic. 9. HIV infection in individuals aged 18 months or older is diagnosed based on a positive HIV antibody test confirmed by a second test using different antigens or operating characteristics, or a positive virological test for HIV components confirmed by a second virological test. 10. For children under 18 months, HIV infection is diagnosed using a positive virological test for HIV components confirmed by a second test conducted more than four weeks after birth. Antibody testing is not recommended for definitive diagnosis in this age group. 11. Surveillance systems should collect data from all relevant sites, including private facilities, community-based organizations, and public health systems, to ensure comprehensive reporting. 12. Reporting sites should maintain an up-to-date list of all facilities providing HIV-related services, including testing, care, and treatment. 13. Data from reporting sites are typically sent to the Ministry of Health at the local level and then to the national level. In some systems, reports may be sent directly to the national level. 14. Laboratories play a critical role in HIV case surveillance by reporting results of diagnostic tests, CD4 counts, and viral load tests. Direct reporting from laboratories improves the quality and completeness of surveillance data. 15. Vital registration systems can be used to identify deaths from HIV-related causes and update records of previously reported cases. Linking electronic vital registration data with surveillance data is essential for accurate reporting. 16. Pharmacy records can provide valuable information for identifying previously unreported patients, ART initiation dates, changes in treatment regimens, and therapy discontinuations. 17. Case report forms should include sufficient information to describe the HIV epidemic by person, place, and time. This includes demographic data, facility information, and details of sentinel events such as diagnosis, ART initiation, and viral suppression. 18. Data management systems for HIV case surveillance should include electronic databases capable of receiving, processing, cleaning, storing, and transferring data. These systems should support manual data entry, de-duplication, quality checks, and data downloads for analysis. 19. Data systems should be able to receive or extract electronic data from digital medical records, laboratories, and pharmacies to ensure efficient and accurate reporting.
